item.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
item.author: D_R_Farrell
item.content:encoded: Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

item.content:encoded: While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia, I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding security that we could improve. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix, so I just went along with it.Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare , the senior product engineer with product that I provably have control over, try to and prevent security issues and ensure compliance with local laws and regulations?“Oh but you can just apply to get an exemption from them here ”First of all, you will have to wait for multiple business days to get a response.You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect!Oh, and oh so give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise!And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval. Approval to appropriately protect your own service!This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I to keep up with the security landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is and I can’t let that happen.If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck off and use an older model that will try to stop you from applying adequate protection.You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models.You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special?Predictably, the only way to make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good.Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place.Or maybe that was your plan all along to get regulators to react and build that moat for you right before your IPO to fend off competitors?Either way, I’m just incredibly frustrated. Big AI labs use the same tools without restrictions to make the security landscape a fucking mess, and then they go and prohibit others from using the same tools to protect themselves from the threats they just created. Fucking asshats.

item.author: datascientist
item.content:encoded: Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware., co-creator of and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World, a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.]Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter📩Below is a polished and edited transcript. All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast. Thanks for having me, Ben. All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI? Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models.That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model.That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models.Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available.Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for.What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives.I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing. Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me.As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for.Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt? So a lot of it comes down to your model choice. You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives. But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small? So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that.But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them.So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory.Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed.Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other. So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it.Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there?For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work? I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement. But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete. I think the biggest barriers are usability. If you look at the benchmarks, it really is no longer a question of model quality. Model quality. Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut.And people are finding that some of the models actually work better, especially if you’re dealing with things like, I don’t want to call it censorship because I feel like that’s a loaded term, but a lot of commercial models have restrictions. They may be intended to prevent a bad use case, but pretty often they can also trip you up even if you’re trying to do something benign.I know a lot of people who work in cybersecurity, for example, who are white hats, but they’re having to work with a lot of stuff where they’re asking questions about malicious actions. With the commercial models, you’re going to keep tripping over the restrictions and the guardrails that are built in with good intentions, but they can really impact your work. Right, right, right. By the way, Pete, the model is one component, but then there are the things surrounding the model, the so-called harness, or even context, memory, knowledge.You can imagine someone, and this is actually something I’ve thought about. You know how people are starting to use these LLMs as therapists or friends, right? Then if you’re going to do that, why not do that on a local model? Why do it on something connected to the cloud?I guess one argument against it is that if you do it locally, you’re responsible for model upgrades and things like that, right? Whereas if you use one of these digital or AI therapist services, they take care of all your history and all of this.Do you think it will become easier for consumers to use local models that are essentially something they trust 100% because they own it? Yeah, I mean, these should be part of the OS. At this point, it’s really an operating system capability that should be available to apps, and I feel like Apple is moving in this direction. I see. Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Yeah, they’re getting the hardware capabilities.The other thing I would say is that local doesn’t have to mean on your laptop. Especially as an enterprise user, you can host on-prem or even spin up a cloud instance that your enterprise has control over, run these models there, and have the same experience.One thing I do want to emphasize is that people are finally having to pay something approaching the real cost of running these models through Anthropic and OpenAI, and hosting locally or hosting on-prem can cost a lot less, too. Although if you look at their consumer offerings, it’s still insanely cheap, right? So $20 a month. I mean, you probably blow through that in a day. Yeah. Especially on the enterprise side, there are a bunch of options that don’t require high-end NVIDIA GPUs. You still need those for training, but for inference, for just running models, as an enterprise, you might already have the capacity lying around. So another important aspect of what you’ve been doing is getting people excited about voice and speech, right? This notion that speech could become a basic computing primitive. It doesn’t necessarily have to feel like some remote service.I still remember you demonstrating to me this voice transcription service in a loud coffee shop near Precita Park. Yes. Right. Yeah. This was several years ago. The accuracy of this thing was insane, and it was running not even on a laptop. I think it was just running on a Raspberry Pi. That’s right. Yeah. And so talk to us about the state of voice as an actual interface, similar to a mouse or a keyboard. Where are we? I think a lot of people are skeptical of voice because they’ve used Siri and Alexa, and it’s a very stilted way of communicating.But the question I often ask people when I’m having a conversation about this stuff and I encounter that resistance is, when you’re sitting on the couch and you’re trying to decide what TV show to watch with your significant other next to you, do you text them or do you talk to them? Apart from a few Gen Z people, almost everybody says talk to them.And so following on from that, it’s like, okay, well, it’s not that people don’t like voice interfaces. It’s that people don’t like bad voice interfaces.So the problem becomes an engineering and user experience problem of how do we make voice interfaces that are pleasant and efficient to use?I think once we do that, voice can really take its place as maybe even a more frequent input medium than the keyboard or touchscreen. Yeah, because I think the general impression people have is that voice and speech are much less deterministic than a keyboard or a touchscreen, right?Although people now interact with their LLMs and misspell things right and left, and it doesn’t seem to matter.But the impression people have is that there’ll be problems with accents, background noise, phrasing, and so on and so forth. So where are we in terms of all of these things? We have solutions available to most of those problems, or at least big improvements. But because there’s no commercial incentive to pull them all together, it really hasn’t hit the mainstream yet.I feel like we’re still dealing with interfaces that are from the previous generation. They haven’t taken on board the LLM era fully, and they’re still suffering from a lot of those problems you listed.And that’s why I think open source can be a really strong lever. So as you’ve been trying to solve a lot of these interface problems, what are some of the lessons that you’ve learned? In fact, maybe some of them might even apply to people who are not working with voice but are just building AI applications.I think one of the things you mentioned to me years ago is that with voice, you don’t have to wait until someone has finished talking to start doing work, right? So what are some of these interface lessons? I think latency is a massive deal. That is something you just don’t get with cloud-based voice interfaces.You’re usually waiting at least a couple of seconds, and that’s long enough for people to wonder if they were actually heard. Yeah, it’s like being on a Zoom call or phone call with someone, and then there’s a pause. Yeah, and they’re just sitting there. It feels like the other person is just sitting there, ignoring you.We know from general user experience research that you really want to be in that 200-millisecond or lower range to feel responsive.I often ask people to imagine that you press a key on the keyboard and it takes two seconds for the key to show up in the window. That would be very awkward. By the way, this is something that people who work with LLMs also have to deal with, but on the output side, right? They want to make sure that the response is not too long. Otherwise, people get impatient, right? Yeah, absolutely.And I do want to mention another thing, which I think might be helpful to people thinking about local AI in general as well.When you’re no longer paying per token, when you’re no longer having to pay to use a voice interface, the way you can use these things, the world of possibilities, becomes so much wider.If you imagine that every app developer had to pay a few cents every time somebody touched an icon on the touchscreen in their app, you would design apps very differently, and a lot of apps wouldn’t exist because of that tax.So once LLMs are built into the OS and just generally available with no cost, and the same with voice, that is not just an incremental change going from a cent to zero. That massively increases the number of viable things that you can use those for. So I imagine, Pete, this is one thing where you’ve done a lot of work, which is basically designing for failure, right? Because in voice, a lot of things can go wrong.What are some of the lessons there in terms of designing your applications with failure in mind? One of my favorite examples of designing for failure is the use of snippets in Google Search.Google Search, from the beginning, knew they couldn’t always get the number one result right. There’s a reason you didn’t just hit “I’m Feeling Lucky.” Yeah, exactly. “I’m Feeling Lucky.” What was genius about their approach was that they actually let you browse, just scan with your eyes.They hoped to get the right result in the top three most of the time, and then you actually narrow it down by looking at the snippets, which tell you enough to click on the right one.And the same thing for voice. The more you can actually read the body language of somebody, as we’re talking, you’re nodding a little bit to indicate what’s happening. Wait a minute, I’m only voice, so you can’t see me. No, I can see. No, no, but in general, right? In general. Well, that’s actually a whole other part of this that I haven’t mentioned.I think having a little camera that’s completely local-only will be a massive part of this. But even without a camera, if you hear supportive noises, or if you start giving a response and somebody reacts, all of those things that we recognize as people, we respond to them and ask more questions versus assuming that we picked the right thing.So really trying to understand all of those cues that we use as people. Some of them are verbal, some of them are body language and visual, but really having them all understood locally.And ensuring that all of those recordings never get recorded, because you can verify that locally. You don’t know what happens to audio and video once you send it up to the cloud. It’s impossible to audit, basically.With local stuff, you can audit. So I’m hoping that opens up the chance to use cameras without increasing the risk to users around privacy. So there are the people who work on speech models, and there’s been a lot of work in that area.In fact, one thing that I think is vastly underappreciated is that people talk about deep learning having an ImageNet moment, but actually the first impressive deep learning models were in speech, before ImageNet, right?So there are people working on speech models. They’ve even talked about end-to-end models, but obviously we have LLMs.For the people who don’t follow this closely, Pete, what’s the relationship between the LLMs and the speech models, or do people not use LLMs? Do they just use speech models? There’s been a massive debate, a split between what I think of as LLM maximalists, who expect everything to be an end-to-end model. “Machines of Loving Grace.” Yes, exactly. And I see usually Anthropic, OpenAI, the big AI companies. Or, you know, the hype machine has to be fed, right? Well, the hype machine has to be fed, and specifically, if the future is end-to-end models, then only the people with the most money can actually build and train them.Now, I’m very strongly in what Berkeley calls the compound AI camp, where you actually build your applications out of multiple models, each of which has a specialized task.So there, instead of having a model that takes speech in and outputs speech audio, you actually have a model that takes speech audio in, converts it to text, feeds that into an LLM, and the LLM then outputs text, which is converted into speech.Now, every time you convert the audio into text, you actually lose a bunch of expressiveness. It’s like a bottleneck of information.You can’t tell how somebody’s asking it, whether they’re asking it with a particular intonation and all of this other stuff. Can’t you, as you’re doing that translation, add metadata? You kind of can, but the whole point of compound AI is that you can take models from different sources and plug them together. So you need some kind of common language, and at the moment, the only thing that all LLMs speak is text input and text output.But the advantages are that you can actually train all of the models independently. With a speech end-to-end model, if you have a new accent, then if it’s a true end-to-end model, you have to do a whole bunch of training.If you have a new input accent, if you have new output voices or new capabilities, if it’s a true end-to-end model, then you’re having to train the whole thing.If it’s not actually, if end-to-end is just a marketing term, then you can train individual components, individual modules separately.But then you’re always agreeing on some settled interface data, like some schema, some language. Even if it’s not text, even if it’s an embedding, you still have to have those fixed points.So yeah, I see end-to-end as much more of a marketing term and something to justify the insane amounts of money that are flowing into these companies. Pete, what about, for our listeners who’ve heard of the term multimodal, right? Gemini is supposed to be multimodal.And coincidentally, I just spoke to someone who works in the visual reasoning and understanding space, and they said actually Gemini is quite poor in terms of understanding video.So what is the state of these multimodal models for your domain, speech? They’re actually often pretty good. Qwen, 1.7 billion, I think it is, actually does a better job than Whisper, a significantly better job on some languages like Mandarin. And the same goes for Gemma.The trouble is that, as general-purpose models, one of the failure cases with Gemma is that you upload audio of some speech, it transcribes it, but it then gets confused by the content of that speech and thinks you’re asking it a question, say, if there was a question in the transcribed speech.So it’s one of these things where you’re trying to use a Swiss Army knife, and it’s a lot easier to use an actual wood saw versus the thing that can do everything and has a little saw attachment with it.So that’s another drawback of the end-to-end models. By the way, obviously you’re the king on this topic. General-purpose models are dead on arrival on the edge, right? I mean, right now, only… For the types of, I mean, some of the really small pieces of hardware that you work on. One of the things I recently did was get a full voice interface where you could connect to Wi-Fi, set the password, and all of this sort of stuff, running on a Raspberry Pi Pico microcontroller that only has 500 kilobytes of RAM.Now, there, you’re never going to have a general-purpose model that’s going to work well for you. But as always… And by the way, one of the things that you’ve also worked on, which is interesting, and which I don’t see a lot of people working on, is taking the browser more seriously, right?So tell us, what’s the motivation behind that, and what has been the reception? Yeah, so it’s tricky because I sometimes think of “We’ve done X, but in the browser” as Hacker News bait, because that always gets a lot of attention as a novelty. But it’s often hard to find practical uses for a lot of these things.With the voice capabilities, with voice input and voice output, what I’ve seen is that it makes it part of the browser operating system, or feel like part of the browser operating system.And once you’re able to transcribe fast and accurately in the browser, it’s a way for people to easily start experimenting with this stuff, and there aren’t any costs for this at the moment.I’ve tried to put a few examples. If you go to Moonshine AI… But the whole notion of using the browser as a point of inference, right? You can imagine other models doing that too, not just yours, which focuses on speech.You can imagine text, I mean, browser inference for text kinds of applications, right? Well, if you’re running Chrome, you’ve already got a very capable model installed. You’ve got a 4-billion-parameter model.I actually did a blog post last year showing how you could just go through Chrome settings and start using it as a chatbot, just typing in the window and getting responses.I think that’s an example of the models becoming part of the operating system, because Chrome is essentially an operating system that sits on top of other operating systems.You can already access that built-in LLM, I think now from any website. It used to be just extensions, but now I think any website can access that from JavaScript.And again, we’re still figuring out what the best use cases are for that. But once it becomes free and you can rely on it being everywhere, I really feel like it’s an iPhone moment for a lot of these new LLM technologies. Or even what you mentioned earlier, which is for people on a laptop, it’ll be part of the OS somehow, right?So looking ahead, Pete, and again, for our listeners, you can follow Pete’s work at Moonshot AI. Moonshine. Ah, Moonshine. Moonshine.ai. And a lot of the work is open source, and you can take advantage of that.So looking ahead, Pete, 12 to 24 months. I hate to put you on the spot. Where are we in terms of, I guess, local or edge models, number one, and number two, just the state of open models in general? Yeah, and I’m always terrible at predictions. But one thing Pete is super good at, for our listeners, is knowing what to work on. So that’s an indication. Just tell us what you’re working on. Yes. So what I see from being deep in the technical side, most of what I end up working on is because I’ve been working on something, and it becomes blindingly obvious that the only reasonable technical solution is X, and so of course I want to work on X.And what I see, and what I’ve seen for the last few years, is the gravitational pull of running this stuff locally or on-prem, or however you want to call it.I often say, “AI wants to be local.”If you think about something like Google Search, you need massive databases, you need armies of servers, you need all of this stuff. If you look at what Claude and ChatGPT are doing, you can run that entirely on one laptop with no internet connectivity.So the shape of these models is perfect for running locally, unlike almost everything else we’ve seen over the last couple of decades, where the cloud has made more sense.So what I expect is all of these pressures: cost for enterprises especially, worries about privacy, worries about capabilities going away, worries about changes.If you built an application on top of a particular version of Claude, even if you’re using the same version in the dropdown, what’s actually happening behind the scenes can change from day to day.So if you want stability, you actually need to host your own, at least in your own cloud infrastructure, if not locally on users’ laptops.And I can keep going on and on. Yeah. And then the other thing, too, is I think a lot of enterprises are recognizing that the moat, or their moat, is really not the model. It’s that compounding loop around the model, right?As you use the model more, you learn more and things like that. So why in the world would you send that to a commercial proprietary model? And why not do fine-tuning on your own model? Yeah, I mean, with that data. Yeah, exactly. And then, as you point out, you actually control your timing and roadmap as well, because you have the model and you know when it’s safe to replace that model with something else.No one is going to replace that model underneath you, right? Nobody’s going to start charging 10 times as much overnight. Right, right, right. And then also, even if they keep the cost the same, they may weaken the model for some reason, right? Yep. Yeah, and it could even be pressure from outside. So by the way, one last question for you, Pete, because obviously you work in a space where you really care about hardware, right?Right now, we’re in a world where Jensen Huang seems to own everything. So what’s your prediction about the state of AI hardware?Are we going to get more diversification? Is AMD going to up its game, or what’s going on in hardware in general? So watch Apple.And disclaimer, I worked at Apple for five years in the 2000s. My wife worked there for 13 years.But if you look at what they’re doing, they’re getting lots of RAM, increasing the RAM speed so that you can actually run models much faster, and they have their own inference-only accelerators.I think with those three, you don’t need a GPU. So you just run everything on a CPU? Well, run everything on a different kind of accelerator. Oh, okay. That’s not a… I see. I see. So CPU… Could actually be pretty fast. Obviously, the… The NVIDIA answer is why we have all the HBM, high-bandwidth memory, on the GPU, right? And I like to think of GPUs as being designed for large batches and training.I like to think of a GPU as trying to use an oil tanker to go and do your shopping.They’re fantastic for these large training jobs, but they’re complete overkill for inference. Inference has a very different shape to the workload that it places on hardware. One thing that I’ve started to pay attention to lately, and it’s very, very early, is high-bandwidth flash. Right. So what’s your take? So that’s another example.I see the massive amount of money that NVIDIA is pulling in, and that also has its own gravitational pull on all of these hardware companies, where they’re looking from a technical side.I don’t have any special insights. I’ve just worked with these things. I know what the workloads look like. Other people are looking at those too, and they’re like, “Oh, I see. We have to stream all of the weights. All of the weights have to be processed for every token.”So if you have something, even if you’re running on the CPU, if you have something that’s got high enough bandwidth to pull the 27 billion weights in a fraction of a second, then the rest of it is fairly easy in terms of actually doing the processing. It’s very much memory-bound, usually.So it’s been awesome seeing high-bandwidth flash, what Apple is doing, increasing the bandwidth on regular RAM.I think we’re going to see a lot of really imaginative solutions now that people understand what the workload looks like. Yeah, and with that, thank you, Pete. And again, the website is moonshine.ai.

item.title: Cooling buildings is overtaking heating them as an energy need, IEA says
item.author: robtherobber
item.content:encoded: The energy needed to cool the world’s buildings is overtaking the energy needed to heat them for the first time in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on November 19, 2026. The IEA, an intergovernmental agency that advises governments on energy, made the finding in the World Energy Outlook 2026, its main annual report. “Already today, for the first time in energy history, demand for cooling in buildings is overtaking that for heating,” the report’s executive summary says.Two forces drive the change: rising incomes and rising temperatures. In emerging and developing economies outside China, 85% of households are exposed to high temperatures for at least part of the year. Fewer than one in five households there own an air conditioner.In the IEA’s main scenario, a projection built on the policies governments have announced, the electricity used for cooling worldwide grows by 1,700 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035. A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours; the kilowatt-hour is the unit on a household power bill. That increase is roughly India’s total electricity demand today.A first in energy historyThe IEA’s press release calls the shift “a striking milestone”: “energy needs to keep buildings cool are now overtaking energy needs for heating them for the first time in history.”Most of this year’s report deals with the oil and gas shock caused by disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The cooling finding comes from another part of the report, on what people use energy for: getting around, heating, cooling and computing. The IEA calls these uses energy services.Of these services, cooling adds the most new demand. Cooling demand in buildings has risen 55% since 2015, the IEA says in its full report. In every scenario the agency models, cooling accounts for more than 40% of the growth in energy services worldwide through 2035.That growth comes mostly from hot countries that are getting richer. It also comes from places where cooling used to be a minor need. The report names Europe, where heat waves and warmer summers are turning cooling into a new source of demand. It cites record heat waves there and strong air conditioner sales in European countries that historically needed little cooling.Who has air conditioning, and who doesn’tAir conditioner ownership varies widely. In Australia, Japan and the United States, around 90% of households own at least one unit, according to the report. In India and Indonesia, fewer than one in five do, despite high cooling needs. Worldwide, around 80% of the population lives in places that need cooling for at least part of the year, and around 40% of households own an air conditioner.In emerging and developing economies outside China, the IEA projects that ownership will rise from under 20% of households today to 32% by 2035 and 45% by 2050. The projection is the same in all its scenarios. The IEA also models a current policies scenario, which counts only the policies already in place. In that scenario, more than 85% of the growth in the world’s stock of home air conditioners over the next decade happens in emerging and developing economies, China included.By the middle of the century, the IEA projects, the world’s buildings will have more cooled floor space than heated floor space.More electricity for cooling, and a heat-wave what-ifIn the main scenario, which the IEA calls the Stated Policies Scenario, the electricity used to cool buildings rises by 1,700 TWh by 2035. It goes from about 3,000 TWh a year today to 4,700 TWh a year.The report also models a “heatwave case,” a what-if kept apart from the main scenario. In it, heat waves become stronger, more frequent and longer, so more households buy air conditioners and use them more. In that case, cooling demand grows by 700 TWh more than in the main scenario by 2035. That is 40% more growth.Cooling also weighs more on power grids than its share of total use suggests. Air conditioners run hardest at the same time, on the hottest days. That drives up peak demand, the highest demand a grid must meet during the year. In the main scenario, cooling makes up only 12% of the world’s electricity demand in 2035, but 30% of peak demand.Peak demand is measured in gigawatts (GW), which count power at a single moment, while terawatt-hours count energy used over a period. Added up across the world’s power systems, it is 4,700 GW today. It grows by about 40% by 2035, in both the main scenario and the current policies scenario. Under current policies, the cooling part of the peak alone grows by 720 GW, more than India’s entire power generating capacity today.In the main scenario, cooling and appliances together add 2,900 TWh of electricity demand by 2035. That is more electricity than the whole European Union uses today. Almost 90% of that growth happens in emerging and developing economies.Heating still consumes more energyMeasured by the fuel and electricity consumed, heating is still well ahead. “Globally, there is less cooling than heating demand, but more electric cooling than electric heating demand,” the report says in its section on buildings. Space heating, which keeps rooms warm, uses about a third of all the energy consumed in buildings, more than any other use.The milestone uses a different yardstick. In the report’s framing, the comparison is about energy services, meaning the comfort delivered. The sentence about cooling overtaking heating sits in the report’s section on demand for energy services. The IEA measures those services as “useful energy”: the energy that does the job people want, such as “the heat produced by a heater.”By our reading, the two findings fit together because of how the equipment works. A boiler burns fuel and loses part of its energy in the process. An air conditioner, like a heat pump, moves heat from one place to another, so it delivers more cooling than the electricity it consumes.The report counts air conditioners and heat pumps as devices whose output exceeds the energy they take in. That, by our reading, is why cooling can overtake heating in the service delivered while heating still consumes more energy.The executive summary puts no number on the crossing itself. It is a result of the IEA’s modeling, and the agency describes the crossing as under way (“is overtaking”). None of the report’s scenarios is a forecast, as the IEA’s executive director, Fatih Birol, said in the press release.In advanced economies, heating remains the largest energy service. It declines only slowly, as better insulation and warmer average temperatures offset the effect of rising incomes.Air conditioners are spreading in the countries where most of the world’s people live. In the IEA’s projections, the share of households that own one in emerging and developing economies outside China more than doubles by 2050. Those households gain comfort, and power grids must carry a bigger load in the hottest hours of the year. Electric trucks, cars and heat pumps add to the load on those grids as well.Electricity already supplied 23% of the energy consumed worldwide in 2025, and the IEA sees that share closing in on 30% by 2035. The agency says at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines are needed over the next ten years. On the supply side, solar covered more of the growth in world energy demand in 2025 than any other source, a first for a renewable source, according to the IEA. In the European Union, solar became the biggest source of electricity over the summer.Efficiency rules also shape demand. Minimum efficiency standards are the legal floor on how efficient an appliance must be to go on sale. For household appliances such as refrigerators, washing machines, lighting and televisions, the IEA calculates that bringing every country up to the strictest standards in force today would save 800 TWh of electricity by 2035, almost half of it from refrigerators alone. For cooling, the current policies scenario keeps those standards at today’s levels, and cooling demand reaches 4,900 TWh by 2035, compared with 4,700 TWh in the main scenario.

item.title: How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40k staff
item.author: liotier
item.content:encoded: The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element, and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users.At The Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it.Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit“Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing.For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control.Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet)With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions. The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms. The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar. Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change.The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly: the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present. the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June. a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform. the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September.The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like.Scaling to 40,000 users brought challengesRolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each.Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on.Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up.Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement.Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically.Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap.The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had.That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together.Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls. Federation goes beyond techThe Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations.No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled.Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission.Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted.Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it.Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance.He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success.

item.title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
item.author: illidan1000
item.content:encoded: It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output.That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch.While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record.Waiting for prices to fall? Use what you have first. DriveVault catalogues every drive you own so you can search them offline, find free space and spot duplicates before you buy. Download FreeNAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash.Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly.Prices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking. TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027.Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories.2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing.Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first.Where Prices Stand in September 2026Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today, shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records. (HDD) (HDD)Source: ComputerBase price check, 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers.The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive, you are feeling the mild end of this.The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns.Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different TimesMost coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways.SSDs follow the chip marketSSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too.Hard drives follow multi-year contractsHard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall.The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts SayTrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026.Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027. The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027.New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down.Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027, with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024.The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop.Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July, with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call, management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity. Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead.Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year, while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call, the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached.Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices.So where does hard drive relief come from?Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments, and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027. As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction.Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once.What Could Change the Timeline AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices. agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers.A flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way.ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard.New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite.Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving.Should You Buy Now or Wait?That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it.You need storage for paid work this yearWaiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices.Your backups are incompleteA failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how.You want a fast SSD upgrade that can waitSSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall.You are stockpiling "just in case"Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased.Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You HaveThe most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged.See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one.Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison, and reclaim the space safely.Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive.Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues.If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhen will hard drive prices come down?Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut.When will SSD prices come down?TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop.Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels?Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast.Should I buy a hard drive now or wait?If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect.Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026?AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking.Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts.The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change.Get more from the drives you already own.DriveVault catalogues your entire drive library so you can search, compare and find free space on any drive, even when it is not plugged in. item.content:encoded: AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in , a solution to compress memory.Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled.Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity.
