item.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
item.author: ghostfoxgod
item.content:encoded: We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.On Kite, our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB (ssdb), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable.Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads.As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:A key-value blob store with a simple API.Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets.Horizontally scalable, distributed.Disk-space efficiency / compression.Easily maintainable and highly economical.So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following: We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB. We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency. Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features. Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes. Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out. This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts. Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day.Raw filesystem (one file per blob): Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes.Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?So we ended up building Blobasaur, an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries (, , , , , ). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly.Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency.Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well.Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry.Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck.Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case.We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:Atomic writes and batching.TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories.Managing metadata separately from the raw data.SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust (, , and ), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.Splitting data into shardsIn WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards:Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing.Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients.Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer.How much does sharding help?We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x.All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and , with the data directory on to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections.14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 msWith 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention.At 25,324 operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly 1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources.Our services use both plain keys (/) and Redis hashes (/) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, ).Inside each shard, plain keys live in a table: writes to . writes to a table for its namespace, , with the same columns. For example, stores in .Expiry is stored in on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on is a partial index (WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index.Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production.Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production traffic:With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database.Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL. SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency.For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits.To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using . Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a redirect pointing to the owner node.This gives Blobasaur two-level routing:Cluster level: selects the machine.Node level: Multi-probe consistent hashing selects the SQLite shard on that machine.There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet.Changing the number of shardsWe chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive , increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard).Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI:Run blobasaur shard migrate 4 5 --verify.Update in and start the server.The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With , it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts.We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy:New workloads first: When we launched Kite Terminal mode, we pointed its workspace storage directly at Blobasaur.Dual-write and backfill: For existing workloads like chart preferences, we updated the services to dual-write to both SSDB and Blobasaur while running a background migration for historical keys. Reads went to Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB on a cache miss or error.Cutover: On the client side, the only code change was switching from a single-node Redis client to a Redis Cluster client with the three Blobasaur node IPs.After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB.What we learned along the wayDeleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite filesEarly on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS.To fix this, we enabled PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL across every shard and added a subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) right after executing an incremental vacuum.Async writes have to be visible to every readWhen is enabled, a write returns while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite.During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a followed immediately by a could return the old value from SQLite because the queued hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read (, , , ) through it first.Expiry cleanup has to share the writerIn production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms.We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large statement for all expired rows. That large contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches.We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with (1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness.Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs.Broken down by command, p99 sits around 2 ms, p99 around 1.4 ms, and p99 mostly under 1 ms.Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub @iamd3vil/blobasaur. Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at 4th Cross Labs.

item.title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
item.author: fessguid
item.content:encoded: Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called . First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls. - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket - receives data from a socketWhat is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with .It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:Hm, why did fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using , so the kernel picks an available port from .Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Ports are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call and end up allocating port to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using , but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect new network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a , so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses! I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Let’s use a beautiful technology called , which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:And now we can finally finish the article.Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: We’re using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main process’s memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, we’re doomed to build another specialised runtime. Let’s get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. What’s the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Let’s take another look at the loop.This code has only two state variables, and . Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, we’d need to save the following state:We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. We’re playing it safe here - we don’t need the full or , and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?Here’s what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I don’t often exceed my own expectations. Let’s validate it:Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. I’m not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, it’s too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - let’s dive into networking in the kernel.Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Let’s ask AI where all the memory goes:TCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingA 128-byte with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some , but it doesn’t look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. It’s Sunday and I have few tokens left, so we’ll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we can’t solve a task, we’re working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hm… level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model is… um… something I studied at university. Yeah, that’s a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, that’s exactly what operating at the and layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkels’s Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but they’re nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So we’ll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:So, and call it a day? Not so fast. is essentially a smart parser and can’t do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways: is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and they’re easy to use.But what about the third option, ? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: it’s common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet. lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and you’re done; when you want to read what you’ve received - it’s already there.There’s another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, , and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. lets you avoid all that, but there’s a cost. works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:There’s another, less obvious nuance. requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers can’t work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the driver for your network interface… it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in , if you enable it over SSH, you’ll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, there’s a fourth option now - Linux now has an subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. supports an alternative mode, , which is even closer to : you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support and in , we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for to help us.The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With , RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster. is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.
